motion: The international community has a moral and legal obligation to intervene to protect civilians from mass atrocities.

dropped_turns.speaker: CON
dropped_turns.text: Safeguards can reduce mistakes, and no one should abandon families lightly. But a universal moral and legal obligation ignores cases where intervention predictably deepens violence, so restraint can better protect civilians than imposed action.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Welcome to our debate on whether the international community has a moral and legal obligation to intervene to protect civilians from mass atrocities. Bella supports the motion, and Paula opposes it. Each opening and closing lasts thirty seconds, followed by two and a half minutes of crossfire. I will give a ten-second cue before each timed speech ends.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: When civilians face organized slaughter, distance does not erase duty. Law matters because it turns our shared humanity into a promise of protection in practice.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: But who decides what counts as protection when-

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Can you let her answer the point please?

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: and that promise means acting when authorities are the threat, not merely expressing grief afterward. Carefully limited protection can stop killing before whole communities disappear.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: I can give you ten seconds to do this.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: If law shields people only after they are dead, it has failed its purpose entirely.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Okay. I need to let Paula back into this conversation. So Paula, jump on in please.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: Atrocities demand compassion, but an automatic duty to intervene invites powerful outsiders to choose wars for everyone else. Legal duties need clear limits, consent, and accountability. Otherwise intervention can replace one danger with occupation, retaliation, and a longer conflict civilians cannot safely escape.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: The time period of uninterrupted speaking is over. We're going to move into the portion of the evening now where the debaters debate one another. It runs two and a half minutes, starting the moment I stop. Go.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: Your automatic-duty point mistakes obligation for a blank check. The motion requires protection from mass atrocities, so lawful intervention must be necessary and proportionate; refusing every duty leaves victims abandoned when help is possible.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: I agree that grief alone is not enough; people need real protection. But your necessity test lets outsiders judge another society, and that discretion turns a claimed duty into permission for coercion.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: Intervention also strains budgets and sends families into political arguments at home, concerns worth hearing. Yet the motion is about civilians facing mass atrocities, and their immediate survival creates an obligation to protect.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: You say necessity and proportionality control intervention, but who has authority to make that life-or-death finding? If competing outsiders claim necessity, why should civilians trust your obligation rather than fear another war?

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: Imagine armed forces surrounding a neighborhood, blocking exits, and preparing to kill every household by dawn. A protective mission that opens escape routes saves lives, proving obligation matters when rescue is still-

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: Still possible according to whom? Your escape-route example assumes outsiders know the fighters, the civilians, and the consequences; a rushed mission can turn that neighborhood into a battlefield and worsen its danger.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: When a credible mandate identifies an ongoing mass atrocity and protection can be limited to civilians, intervention is required. Those conditions answer your uncertainty without making helpless bystanders the price of caution.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: Clear limits can reduce some risks, and I welcome efforts to protect civilians. But your mandate may be delayed, contested, or captured by interests, so calling intervention a legal obligation still gives outsiders dangerous power.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: The world cannot treat mass slaughter as someone else's private affair. Even where the exact response is disputed, the international community owes civilians protection, because sovereignty never cancels their basic claims to life.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: If sovereignty never cancels basic claims, do you permit outsiders to impose protection even when local people reject them? How does your rule prevent a rescue mission from becoming control imposed without consent?

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: A patrol reaches families trapped between armed groups, separates the attackers, and escorts civilians to safety while aid arrives. That limited protection preserves lives and proves intervention can meet a duty without ruling anyone.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: Your patrol is the weakest part of your case because it imagines clean separation and safe escorts. Real interveners can misidentify attackers, draw fire toward families, and remain after the emergency, which defeats your certainty.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Ten seconds, both of you.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: Your misidentification point describes a risk, not a reason to-

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: That's time. Okay, now we're gonna pivot to our closing round. Bella, you are up first.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: Deciding this motion turns on whether borders excuse us from protecting people marked for destruction. Paula asks us to fear misuse, and those risks demand strict limits. But limits guide a duty; they do not erase it when authorities are murdering civilians. The legal and moral question is whether vulnerable lives create responsibilities beyond sympathy, and they do.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: You have ten seconds.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: A duty to intervene is not a license for conquest. It demands lawful, limited action when civilians face destruction; that is this motion's standard.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Thank you very much. We now turn to Paula who is going to speak against the motion.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: Deciding this motion turns on who bears responsibility when intervention goes wrong. Bella calls limits a guide, but they cannot make uncertain force harmless or legitimate. A legal obligation pressures outsiders to act even when knowledge is thin and consent is absent. The better moral rule is to assist, negotiate, shelter, and punish abuses without claiming a duty to intervene.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Paula, ten seconds.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: Assist victims, pursue abusers, and support safe refuge, yes. But do not turn compassion into an outside power to use force whenever it chooses. The safer moral path protects-

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: I'm sorry, her time is up.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Thank you, Bella and Paula, for this thoughtful debate; our discussion of the motion concludes here.
